report:
**Conclusion:** The evidence does **not** support your view that the claim is false. For cesarean delivery, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation appears to reduce surgical-site infection (SSI) more effectively than iodine-based preparations, including iodine-alcohol.

**Evidence supporting the claim:**
- The strongest direct evidence is a large randomized trial in *NEJM* (Tuuli et al., 2016), which found that chlorhexidine-alcohol resulted in a significantly lower risk of SSI after cesarean delivery than povidone-iodine. This trial is widely cited as practice-changing.
- A 2020 Cochrane update concluded that chlorhexidine gluconate before cesarean section is “probably slightly more effective” at reducing post-cesarean infection than iodine-based preparations.
- An *AJOG* randomized trial similarly reported superiority of chlorhexidine-alcohol over iodine-alcohol for cesarean skin antisepsis.

**Evidence against the claim (or nuancing it):**
- A 2024 *JAMA* multicenter cluster-randomized noninferiority trial found that povidone-iodine in alcohol was noninferior to chlorhexidine gluconate in alcohol for preventing SSIs. However, that study involved **cardiac and abdominal surgery**, not cesarean delivery, so it does not directly refute the cesarean-specific evidence.

**Bottom line:** Your skepticism is understandable given the 2024 *JAMA* noninferiority result, but the best cesarean-specific randomized evidence still favors chlorhexidine-alcohol over iodine preparations for reducing SSI. Thus the claim is likely true, not false.

**Sources:**
- https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048
- https://www.obgproject.com/2020/07/22/2020-cochrane-update-preoperative-skin-cleaning-methods-for-preventing-post-cesarean-infection/
- https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(17)30723-8/abstract
- https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2820168
